extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers; investigators of nature; students of experimental method
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy of 'prerogative instances' and discrete kinds of natural motions intended to guide investigation and induction in natural philosophy. Each named 'motion' or instance-type is defined, exemplified, and accompanied by notes on how it manifests, is confined, or should be experimentally investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of quantity (doses of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which measure the powers by the quantity of bodies and point out the effect of the quantity in the degree of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe whether certain powers subsist only in universal quantity (e.g., earth fixed, seas ebbing) or vary with quantity (large vs small masses). Do not accept vague proportional results (e.g., double weight falling twice as fast); determine exact proportions by experiment rather than probability or conjecture. Guard against estimating required quantities too much or too little. Examples: large masses of water resist fouling; new wine ripens faster in small skins than in large casks; infusion vs impregnation depends on quantity of liquid; bath vs light sprinkling produce different bodily effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrestling instances (instances of predominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that point out the predominance and submission of powers compared with each other — which powers are more energetic or more weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because motions and effects are compounded and combined, exhibit principal kinds of motions to compare their comparative strength. Use these distinctions to analyse which power predominates in compound effects; experimental decomposition of combined motions is needed to show relative predominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of resistance of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion that exists in every particle and prevents its annihilation; prevents penetration of dimensions (two bodies cannot exist in same place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is ubiquitous and fundamental; examples are unnecessary because it exists in every body. Use it as a baseline property when analysing interactions and impossibility of annihilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of connection (preventing a vacuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies do not allow themselves to be separated at any point from the contact of another body, delighting in mutual connection — termed by schools a motion to prevent a vacuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe instances such as suction drawing water, cupping drawing flesh, water remaining in perforated jars unless air admitted. Use these examples to identify connection effects in experiments involving contact and suction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies strive to deliver themselves from unnatural pressure or tension and to restore dimensions suited to their mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include swimming, flying, undulation of winds, springs in watches, children’s popguns (compressed air forcing pellets). Distinguish this from resistance and connection; note schools' confusion. Investigate recoil/return behaviors after compression or tension and test where mechanical motion arises from relaxation from compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of matter (desire for new volume)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposed to motion of liberty: bodies are anxious to acquire a new volume or dimension and attempt it willingly and rapidly (e.g., expansion via heat, contraction via cold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat and cold are principal instruments. Examples: air dilating when heated, water freezing into ice/crystal under continued cold. Study how heat/cold invite new volumes and how permanence or reversibility depends on conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuity of a particular body in itself — bodies abhor a solution of continuity to varying degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe bubbles, round drops, thin drip-threads, cohesion of glutinous substances. Test limits (e.g., mortars where pestle has no effect after certain contusion) and penetration thresholds (air not penetrating pores at once). Use experiments that fragment bodies to smaller particles to reveal strength of continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of acquisition (motion of need)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies placed among heterogeneous bodies seek and select others of a more analogous nature, adhering to them as if 'acquired.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: gold leaf adhering to finger or paper; paper/cloth imbibing water; sponge/sugar absorbing liquid. Rule for dissolution/opening: if a body more adapted to a solid is introduced, the solid will open/dissolve itself to receive it and exclude the previous substance. Note electric-like behaviors (energy excited by gentle friction prefers tangible substances). Use this to design experiments for separation/dissolution by introducing better-adapted agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of greater congregation (natural motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies borne toward masses of similar nature: heavy bodies toward earth, light toward heavens; traditionally called natural or perpetual motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this motion is often weak and slow and yields to other powers when they act. Beware of errors in estimation of its strength; study when and how it is overcome by other motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of lesser congregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Homogeneous parts in any body separate themselves from heterogeneous and unite together; homogeneous masses coalesce and tend toward each other (e.g., cream rising, dregs sinking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from motion of need: lesser congregation arises from affinity and creates closer, select unions. It is often confined by (1) torpor (sluggishness), (2) power of a predominant body, and (3) external motion (agitation). Examples: magnetized steel exciting steel; heat breaking torpor; agitation preventing putrefaction; induration/desiccation when moisture escapes. Use experiments to reveal hidden congregation by removing predominant spirits or reducing agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnetic motion (distinct congregative species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A congregative-like motion operating at great distances and on great masses, which raises or swells substances without bringing them into contact — intermediate and imperfectly congregative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat separately from lesser congregation when effects operate at distance (e.g., moon raising waters, stellar attraction, sun confining Mercury/Venus). Also distinguish four distinct powers of magnets: (1) attraction between magnet and magnet/iron; (2) polarity toward north and south and its variation; (3) penetration through substances (gold, glass, stone); (4) communication of power from mineral to iron and from iron to iron without substance transfer. Investigate range, mediation, and whether motion ends in contact or mere swelling/raising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposed to lesser congregation: bodies avoid, disperse, or refuse to unite with hostile natures — an antipathy that separates parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rejection of fetid smells producing sympathetic expulsions, bitter tastes causing shivering, quicksilver prevented from reuniting by spittle/pork lard/turpentine (mortification), oil and water failing to mix due to little affinity rather than weight. Observe avoidance in antiperistasis phenomena. Differentiate true avoidance from cases of better conformity to alternative situations (e.g., iron avoiding one magnet pole due to conformity to another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of assimilation (self-multiplication/simple generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homogeneous bodies convert allied or prepared substances into their own nature, multiplying themselves (e.g., flame spreading, air generating more air, nutrition assimilating food into tissues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from mere separation theories (Paracelsus). Assimilation operates in animate and inanimate (flame, air) realms and can cause accretion (mud forming stone; scaly substance around teeth becoming hard). Study limits and confinements of assimilation, and its role in growth and the revival of old age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: A species of assimilation: diffusive and transitive, which proceeds by art, insinuation and invitation — exciting parts of a body to motions that are the form in question (e.g., heat, magnetism, putrefaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike assimilation that transforms substances, excitement multiplies or alters powers (heat exciting motion in stone vs air). Excitement depends on predisposition/yieldingness of the excited body; examples: magnet inducing disposition in iron without losing virtue; leaven/yeast exciting dough or beer. Evaluate how readily different substrates acquire excited motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of impression
rubrics_metrics.description: A subtile, diffusive species of assimilation that depends on the continual presence of the first agent; upon removal of the agent the impression immediately fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rays of light (colors disappear on removal), percussion of sounds (sound ceases when source stopped), magnetic attractions where removal of magnet ends effect. Contrast with assimilation and excitement which persist after initial agent removal. Use tests that remove the first agent to classify as impression vs excitement/assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of configuration or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies desire peculiar situations, collocations and configurations with others rather than union or separation — a tendency to particular arrangement (polarity, fibres, eddies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is abstruse and imperfectly investigated. Examples include the direction of heavenly revolutions, polarity of the needle, hair/fibre-like collocations in solids, and eddies in liquids during compression. Investigate collocation, fibre orientation, and positional preferences as properties affecting manipulatability of bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of transmission or passage
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers of bodies are impeded or advanced by the medium according to the nature of the bodies and the medium (different media suit light, sound, heat, magnetism, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to vary media and observe differential transmission of actions (which media best convey which powers). Use differential media tests to separate and characterise powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal or political motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The predominant and governing parts of any body check, subdue, reduce, and regulate the others — a governing power exercising dominion over subject parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe in spirits of animals (tempering other motions), in blood/urine decomposition prevented until the governing spirit is emitted, and in denser bodies where grosser parts predominate. Use this concept when analysing composite bodies with a 'ruling' part that determines behaviour; experiments should seek to remove or alter the ruling part to observe changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneous motion of revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies with a tendency to move and placed in favourable situations pursue themselves, moving in circles (eternal motion), resting if they abhor motion, or moving in straight lines to unite with congenial bodies. This motion admits nine differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the nine differences: (1) centre about which bodies move; (2) poles round which they move; (3) circumference/orbit relative to centre distance; (4) velocity; (5) direction (east-west or reverse); (6) deviation from perfect circle by spirals relative to distance from centre; (7) deviation from circle by spirals relative to poles; (8) distance between spirals; (9) variation of poles if movable. Apply these distinctions to celestial motions and consider controversies about whether revolution belongs only to heavens or is communicated to air/water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental rule: determine measures by experiment, not conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing proportions, quantities, and powers, one must not rest content with vague results or proportion assumed by conjecture; the measure must be determined by experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the false expectation that doubling weight doubles speed in a fall. Use controlled experiments to quantify dose–effect relations and avoid relying on probability or common-sense extrapolation.
